listeningParts.title: Volunteering at a food bank
listeningParts.contextDescription: A woman phones a community food bank because she wants to become a volunteer.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Hello, Riverside Food Bank, this is Gary speaking.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Oh, hi. I saw a poster in the library saying you need more volunteers, and I'd like to find out how I can help.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: That's great, thank you for calling. We always need more people, especially at this time of year. Have you volunteered anywhere before?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Not at a food bank, no. I used to help at my children's school, listening to young children read, but that was a few years ago. I've just retired from my job, so now I've got a lot more free time.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Well, you'd be very welcome. Let me tell you a bit about how we work. People bring us donations of food, mainly tins and packets, and we also collect food from two supermarkets every week. Volunteers check and sort everything, and then we pack it into bags for families who've been sent to us by doctors, schools or social workers.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: I see. And when do you need people?

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: We're open three days a week: Monday, Wednesday and Saturday. Which days would suit you?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Wednesdays are difficult, because I look after my grandson that day. But Saturday would be fine.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Saturday's perfect. That's our busiest day, actually. There are two shifts: the morning shift is from nine until twelve, and the afternoon shift is from twelve until three.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: I'd prefer the morning, if that's possible.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: No problem. On Saturday mornings, most volunteers work in the warehouse at the back, sorting donations. We need to check the dates on everything, because we can't give out food that's out of date. Then later in the morning, some people move to the front and help with packing the bags.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That sounds fine. Is there anything I need to wear?

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Just comfortable clothes. But you must wear closed shoes, like trainers or boots, because people sometimes drop heavy tins. Sandals aren't allowed in the warehouse. We give everyone an apron, so you don't need to bring one.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Okay. Do I need any training?

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Yes, all new volunteers come to a short induction session first. It takes about ninety minutes, and we explain health and safety, how to lift boxes properly, and how to talk to the people who visit us. The next one is on Thursday evening at six thirty.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Ninety minutes. That's fine. Where do I go?

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: We're at forty-two Mill Lane. That's M-I-L-L, Mill Lane. It's the old church hall, opposite the fire station. If you come by car, you can park in the car park behind the church. It's free on weekdays and Saturdays.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Lovely. What else do you need from me?

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: I'll take your name and number now, and then I'll send you a form. On the form, you need to give the name of someone who can give you a reference, such as a previous employer. It's just a short note to say you're reliable.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That's easy. My old manager will do that.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Great. So, what's your name, please?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: It's Margaret Hargreaves.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Could you spell your surname for me?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Yes, it's Hargreaves: H-A-R-G-R-E-A-V-E-S.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Thank you. And a phone number?

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Lovely. One more thing: we're also looking for drivers to collect food from the supermarkets on Monday mornings. Is that something you might be interested in?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Maybe later. I'd like to start with the sorting first and see how I get on.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: That makes sense. Many of our volunteers start with one shift and then do more. Some of them have been with us for over ten years! Well, thank you, Margaret. I'll see you at the induction on Thursday.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Thanks, Gary. See you then.

listeningParts.title: A river clean-up day
listeningParts.contextDescription: An organiser gives instructions to volunteers at the start of a community river clean-up.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Good morning, everyone! Can you all hear me at the back? Great. Welcome to the fifth Millbrook River Clean-Up. My name's Jess, and I'm one of the organisers. Thank you so much for giving up your Sunday morning. We've got more than eighty volunteers here today, which is a record. Last year we had about fifty.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Before we start, I'll explain how the morning will work and give you some safety information. Please listen carefully, because the river is beautiful, but it can also be dangerous.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: First, the plan. We'll work from now until twelve thirty, and then we'll all meet back here at the bandstand for lunch. The lunch is free, and it's been provided by the bakery on the high street, so please thank them if you go in there. There are vegetarian options too.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Now, safety. Everyone must wear one of the yellow high-visibility vests, which are in the boxes next to me, and everyone must wear gloves. Never pick up anything sharp, like broken glass or needles, with your hands, even if you're wearing gloves. If you find something like that, don't touch it. Just mark the place with one of the small orange flags and tell your team leader, who'll deal with it.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Please don't go into the water at all, even where it looks shallow. The river bottom is very muddy, and it's easy to get stuck. If you see something in the water that you'd like us to remove, tell your team leader. And please stay on the path side of the fence near the old mill, because the bank there is not safe.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: We have a first-aid tent next to the car park. It's the white tent with a green cross on it. If you cut yourself, even slightly, please go there and get it cleaned, because river water can carry infections.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Right, you've all been put into teams of about ten, and each team has a different job. Your team name is on the sticker you got when you signed in. Let me explain what each team will be doing.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: The Kingfisher team will be working along the riverbank between the bridge and the old mill, collecting general litter. That's the longest section, so you're the biggest team. You'll each have a litter picker and two bags, a black one for rubbish and a clear one for things that can be recycled, such as cans and plastic bottles.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: The Otter team will be in the children's playground and the picnic area. This is a good team for families with young children, because it's away from the water. Your job is mainly to collect small items, such as sweet wrappers and bottle tops.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: The Heron team has a special job this year. You'll be counting and recording everything you collect on a form, so that we can send the information to a national charity that studies river pollution. So it's a bit slower, but it's really useful.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: The Badger team will be cutting back plants that are growing over the footpath. You'll be working with two staff members from the council's parks department, who'll show you how to use the tools safely.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: And finally, the Swan team will stay here at the bandstand. You'll be weighing the full bags as the other teams bring them back, so that we know how much rubbish we've collected in total. Last year it was over six hundred kilograms! Then, at about twelve, you'll help to set up the tables for lunch.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: One last thing. We'd love to share some photos of today on our website and in the local newspaper. If you don't want to appear in any photos, please tell the photographer, who's wearing a red cap. Okay, team leaders, please hold up your signs, and let's get started!

listeningParts.title: A survey on student volunteering
listeningParts.contextDescription: Two students, Aisha and Ben, talk to their tutor about a survey they carried out on volunteering at their college.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Hi, Aisha, hi, Ben. Come in and sit down. So, you've finished your survey on student volunteering. How did it go?

dialogue.speaker: Aisha
dialogue.text: Really well, thanks. We wanted to find out how many students at the college do voluntary work, what kind of work they do, and why some students don't volunteer at all.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: And how did you collect your answers?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.text: We used an online questionnaire. At first we planned to stand in the canteen and ask people questions face to face, but we decided online would be quicker, and people might be more honest if they didn't have to talk to us.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good thinking. How many people answered?

dialogue.speaker: Aisha
dialogue.text: We sent it to about six hundred students, and two hundred and twelve people completed it. We were quite pleased with that.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: So am I. That's a good number for a project like this. How did you get so many replies?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.text: We offered a prize. Everyone who finished the questionnaire could enter a draw to win a voucher for the college café. I think that helped a lot.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Okay. And what were the main results?

dialogue.speaker: Aisha
dialogue.text: Well, about a third of the students said they'd done some volunteering in the last year. That was more than we expected, actually. We thought it would be around one in five.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Interesting. What kind of volunteering was most common?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.text: Sport was the biggest group. Lots of students help to coach children's football or swimming teams at the weekend. The second biggest was helping in charity shops, and then working with animals, for example at the animal rescue centre near the college.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: And why did they say they volunteer?

dialogue.speaker: Aisha
dialogue.text: We gave them a list of reasons and asked them to choose the most important one. The top answer was that they enjoy helping other people. But the second was that it looks good on a CV, which isn't surprising, because many of them are applying for jobs or university places.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.text: And quite a few said they started volunteering because a friend asked them to come along. We hadn't really thought about that, but it seems to be important.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Yes, research often shows that being asked is one of the main reasons people start. What about the students who don't volunteer?

dialogue.speaker: Aisha
dialogue.text: The biggest reason was lack of time. Lots of students have part-time jobs as well as their studies. The next reason was that they didn't know how to find opportunities. Some of them said they'd like to volunteer, but they didn't know where to start.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's a useful finding, because it's something the college could do something about. Did you include any recommendations?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.text: Yes. We suggest the college should have a volunteering fair at the start of each year, where local charities can come in and talk to students. And we'd like a noticeboard on the college website with a list of opportunities.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Both good ideas. Now, were there any problems with the survey?

dialogue.speaker: Aisha
dialogue.text: One question was confusing. We asked how many hours a month people volunteer, but some people answered in hours a week, so we had to remove some answers.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That happens a lot. Mention it in your report, and explain what you'd change next time. Is there anything else?

dialogue.speaker: Aisha
dialogue.text: We also wondered whether we should have asked about the types of organisation people volunteer for. Quite a few people mentioned animal shelters and sports clubs in the comments box, but we hadn't given those as options.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That would be a useful improvement for a follow-up survey. Include the comments as examples in an appendix.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.text: Not really. Oh, the student magazine asked if they could publish our results. Is that all right?

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's fine, as long as you don't include any names. I'd love to see it. Well done, both of you.

listeningParts.title: Henry Dunant and the birth of the Red Cross
listeningParts.contextDescription: A lecture in a history course about how the Red Cross movement began.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good morning, everyone. Today we're going to look at the beginnings of one of the largest volunteer organisations in the world: the Red Cross. Its story begins with one man and one terrible day.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The man was Henry Dunant, who was born in Geneva, in Switzerland, in 1828. He was a businessman, and in the eighteen-fifties he had business interests in Algeria, in North Africa. In June 1859, he travelled to northern Italy, hoping to meet the French emperor, Napoleon the Third, to ask for help with his business.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: At that time, France and its ally were fighting the Austrian army in northern Italy. On the evening of the twenty-fourth of June, Dunant arrived near the small town of Solferino, just after a huge battle had taken place there. Around forty thousand soldiers had been killed or wounded in a single day. What shocked Dunant most was that thousands of wounded men were simply left lying on the battlefield, because the armies had very few doctors and almost no medical supplies.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Dunant forgot all about his business. He went to the nearby town of Castiglione, where many of the wounded had been taken, and organised the local people, many of them women, to help. They brought water and food, washed and dressed wounds, and wrote letters for dying soldiers to their families. Importantly, Dunant insisted that they should care for soldiers from both sides equally. The local women repeated a phrase in Italian which means 'all are brothers'.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: When Dunant returned to Geneva, he couldn't forget what he had seen. In 1862, he wrote a short book called A Memory of Solferino. In it, he described the battle and its terrible results, and he made two important suggestions. First, every country should set up a society of trained volunteers who would be ready to care for wounded soldiers in times of war. And second, countries should sign an international agreement to protect these volunteers and the wounded.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The book was a great success and was translated into many languages. In 1863, Dunant and four other men from Geneva formed a committee to put his ideas into action. This group later became the International Committee of the Red Cross. Just one year later, in 1864, the representatives of twelve countries signed the first Geneva Convention, which said that medical staff and the wounded must be protected and treated as neutral.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The volunteers needed a symbol, so that soldiers would recognise and respect them. They chose a red cross on a white background. This is the Swiss flag with the colours reversed, as a way of honouring Switzerland, where the movement began. Later, in the eighteen-seventies, during a war with Russia, the Ottoman Empire began to use a red crescent instead, and today the Red Crescent is used in many countries.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Sadly, Dunant's own life did not go well. His business in Algeria failed, and in 1867 he went bankrupt. He had to leave Geneva, and for many years he lived in poverty, almost forgotten. Then, in 1895, a journalist found him living in a small care home in the Swiss village of Heiden and wrote an article about him. People around the world were reminded of what he had done, and in 1901, Dunant was awarded the very first Nobel Peace Prize, which he shared with a French campaigner for peace.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Today, the Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement has national societies in more than one hundred and ninety countries, and it depends on millions of volunteers. Every year, on the eighth of May, World Red Cross and Red Crescent Day is celebrated. That date was chosen because it was Dunant's birthday. Next time, we'll look at how the movement's work has changed since the two World Wars.

readingPassages.title: The story of the charity shop
paragraphs: Walk down almost any high street in Britain today and you will find at least one charity shop. These shops sell second-hand clothes, books, toys and furniture that members of the public have given away, and the money they make goes to a good cause, such as medical research, help for homeless people or aid for poor countries. There are now more than ten thousand charity shops in the United Kingdom, and they have become a familiar part of everyday life. But how did they begin?

One early example opened in 1899, when the Wolverhampton Society for the Blind started a shop on Victoria Street in the English city of Wolverhampton. It was rather different from a modern charity shop. Instead of selling goods that had been given away, it sold baskets, mats and chair seats that had been made by blind and partially sighted people. The shop gave them a way to earn money from their work, and it also helped to raise money for the society.

The idea of selling donated goods became much more common during the Second World War. In 1941, the Red Cross opened a shop on Old Bond Street in London, where people could give items they no longer needed so that they could be sold to raise money for the war effort. The idea quickly spread. Over the next few years, the Red Cross opened more than two hundred permanent shops, as well as many temporary ones, across the country.

The organisation most closely linked with charity shops today, however, is Oxfam. It began in 1942 as a small group of people in the city of Oxford who called themselves the Oxford Committee for Famine Relief. At that time, Greece was occupied by enemy forces, and the Allied countries had blocked ships from reaching it. As a result, many Greek people were starving. The committee campaigned for food to be allowed through and collected money to help.

After the war ended, the committee continued its work, sending help to people in Europe who had lost their homes. In the late 1940s, it opened a shop on Broad Street in the centre of Oxford, where people could bring clothes and other goods to be sold. The shop was a great success, and it is still open today. Over the following decades, the committee, which officially took the shorter name Oxfam in 1965, opened hundreds of shops, and many other charities copied its example.

Charity shops can make money for several reasons. First, almost everything they sell has been donated, so they do not have to buy stock. Second, most of the people who work in them are volunteers, who give their time for free, although larger shops usually have a paid manager. Third, in the United Kingdom, charity shops pay much lower business taxes than ordinary shops. This means that even when items are sold for low prices, a large part of the money can go to the charity.

Over time, charity shops have changed. Many now sell some new goods, such as cards and fair trade products, as well as second-hand items. Some specialise in one type of product, such as furniture, wedding dresses or books. Oxfam, for example, says that it is the largest seller of second-hand books in Europe. Many charities also sell donated goods online, which allows rare or valuable items to reach buyers who will pay a higher price for them.

Charity shops are not without their critics. Some owners of small businesses say that it is unfair for them to compete with shops that pay lower taxes and do not have to pay most of their staff. However, supporters point out that charity shops give a second life to clothes and other goods that might otherwise be thrown away, which is good for the environment. They also give volunteers, many of them retired people or young people looking for work experience, a chance to meet others and learn new skills. For many people, a charity shop is not just a place to buy a cheap jacket but a small but important part of the community. Whatever the arguments, charity shops remain a familiar part of town centres, and for many shoppers a visit to one is now a normal part of looking for a bargain.

readingPassages.title: Is volunteering good for you?
paragraphs: Every year, millions of people around the world give up their free time to help others without being paid. They coach children's sports teams, visit elderly neighbours, plant trees, answer phones for helplines and serve food in community kitchens. Most people volunteer because they want to help, but a growing amount of research suggests that the volunteers themselves may also benefit in important ways. Scientists, doctors and governments have become increasingly interested in these benefits, partly because volunteering costs very little and is available to almost everyone. If helping others really does make people happier and healthier, it could be a simple way to improve the lives of millions of people.

One of the most common benefits that volunteers report is a feeling of happiness and satisfaction. Many people describe a warm, positive feeling after helping someone, and this has sometimes been called a 'helper's high'. Studies that ask people about their wellbeing have often found that volunteers say they are more satisfied with their lives than people who do not volunteer. Doing something useful for others seems to give people a sense of purpose. This may be especially important for people who have recently retired from work or whose children have left home, because these changes can leave them feeling that they are no longer needed.

Volunteering can also help people to make friends and feel part of a community. Loneliness is a serious problem in many countries, especially among older people and people who live alone. Working alongside others towards a shared goal gives people a natural reason to talk and spend time together. For people who have recently moved to a new area, volunteering can be one of the quickest ways to get to know their neighbours. Volunteers often say that the friendships they make are among the most valuable things they get from their work, and some of these friendships last for many years.

There is also some evidence of benefits to physical health. In 2013, researchers at the University of Exeter Medical School in England looked at the results of many earlier studies. They found that, in studies which followed people over a number of years, volunteers were less likely to die during the study period than people who did not volunteer. Volunteering was also linked to lower levels of depression. Other studies have suggested that older volunteers, in particular, tend to stay more physically active, perhaps because their work involves walking, carrying things or simply leaving the house more often.

However, the researchers were careful to explain that these results do not prove that volunteering itself makes people healthier. It is possible that people who are already healthy, active and well connected are simply more likely to volunteer in the first place. In other words, good health might lead to volunteering, rather than the other way round. To be more certain, scientists need more studies in which people are chosen at random to volunteer or not, and then followed over time.

For younger people, one important benefit of volunteering is the chance to develop skills that are useful at work. Volunteers may learn how to work in a team, communicate with the public, organise events or handle money. These experiences can give them confidence and can also be mentioned on a CV or in a job interview. Some employers say they value voluntary work because it shows that a person is reliable and willing to take responsibility. For students who are not sure what career they want, volunteering can also be a way to try out different kinds of work, such as teaching, nursing or working outdoors, before making a decision.

Volunteering is not always a positive experience, though. Some volunteers find that they are given boring tasks or that they are not properly trained or supported. Others take on too much and begin to feel tired and stressed, especially if their work involves helping people in difficult situations. Experts say that good organisations should give volunteers clear information about what they will do, offer training and make sure they feel appreciated. Something as simple as saying thank you, or inviting volunteers to a small celebration at the end of the year, can make a big difference to whether people decide to continue.

So, is volunteering good for you? The answer seems to be that it often is, although perhaps not in every case. Most people who volunteer say they get a lot out of it, and there are good reasons to think that helping others can improve our happiness and our connections with other people. Perhaps the best advice is to choose an activity that you enjoy and that fits into your life, rather than one that you feel you ought to do.

readingPassages.title: Should volunteering be compulsory for students?
paragraphs: In many countries, governments and schools are keen to encourage young people to help in their communities. Some have gone further and made a certain amount of community service a requirement for finishing school. Supporters say this teaches young people to care about others, while critics argue that forced 'volunteering' is not really volunteering at all. Looking at some of the programmes that exist around the world can help us to think about this question.

In the United States, the state of Maryland became, in 1992, the first state to require all students to complete community service before they could finish high school. Students there must do seventy-five hours of service, which can include helping at food banks, tutoring younger children or working on environmental projects. Many schools in other states have since introduced their own requirements, although most states have not made it a rule for every school.

In Canada, the province of Ontario introduced a similar rule in 1999. Since then, every student must complete forty hours of community involvement in order to receive a secondary school diploma. Students can choose their own activities, as long as they are unpaid and benefit the community. Some schools help students to find suitable placements, while others leave it to the students and their families.

Service is also part of some international qualifications. Students taking the International Baccalaureate Diploma, which is offered by schools in many countries, must complete a programme called Creativity, Activity, Service, usually known as CAS. As part of this programme, students take part in service activities and write about what they have learned from them. The aim is to help students think about their own role in the wider world.

Other countries have chosen to encourage young people rather than force them. In England, the National Citizen Service, which was introduced in 2011, offers teenagers aged fifteen to seventeen a programme of activities that includes planning and carrying out a project in their local community. It is completely voluntary. In Germany, after compulsory military service was suspended in 2011, a Federal Volunteer Service was created, which gives people of all ages the chance to work for a period in areas such as social care, sport or the environment. Taking part is entirely voluntary, and the programme is designed to be affordable, so that young people from all kinds of families can join.

France has taken a different approach again. In 2019, it launched a programme called the Universal National Service, which brings together young people of around fifteen to seventeen from different backgrounds for a period of group activities, followed by a mission helping an organisation in the community. The government has discussed making it compulsory for all young people, but this has been controversial, and so far it has remained mostly voluntary.

So, do compulsory programmes work? Researchers have reached mixed conclusions. Some studies suggest that students who are required to do community service are just as likely to volunteer later in life as those who are not, or even more likely. Others have found that being forced to help can make some young people less keen to volunteer in the future, especially if the activities feel pointless. Much seems to depend on the quality of the experience and on whether students are allowed to choose what they do. Part of the difficulty is that it is hard to measure the long-term effects of such programmes, since students who choose to volunteer may already be different in important ways from those who do not. Researchers also point out that the quality of the experience seems to matter a great deal: well-organised placements that give students real responsibility appear to have more positive effects than tasks that feel pointless.

In my view, schools are right to make some form of community service part of education. Many young people never try volunteering simply because nobody asks them, and a requirement can open doors that would otherwise stay closed. However, I believe the number of hours should be modest, and students must be given a real choice of activities. It is also important that students have time to talk about what they have done. Without this, I think community service risks becoming just another box to tick, rather than an experience that changes the way young people see the world.
